feedback: If you predicted the moving crate would stop when forces are balanced: balanced forces give a zero resultant, meaning no CHANGE — an already-moving object keeps its steady speed. Here friction is treated as negligible, so no other horizontal force is present to slow it.

If you expected the crate to reach a fixed fast speed and stay there while the rightward arrow stays longer: a constant unbalanced force pointing along the motion keeps accelerating the crate, so its speed keeps climbing for as long as that force acts.
If you read the resultant as an additional push: notice the overlay replaces the original arrows — it is their single combined effect, not an extra force.

For the angled case (crate starting from rest): the resultant is built head-to-tail; it is not the bisector of the two arrows, and it is not found by adding their lengths as plain numbers. Starting from rest, the crate accelerates along the resultant; if it were already moving in another direction, an angled resultant would curve its path rather than instantly align travel with the force.
activities.intendedInsight: A zero resultant means no change in motion — which includes continuing to move at a steady speed, not only being at rest. A sustained unbalanced resultant keeps changing the motion; when it points along the direction of travel the speed keeps climbing, showing that force governs CHANGE of motion rather than speed itself. The resultant is the single equivalent of the combined forces, and for non-collinear forces it is found by head-to-tail (vector) addition. This model assumes negligible horizontal friction, so the drawn arrows are the only horizontal forces.
learnerActions: Set the crate moving steadily to the right. In this model horizontal friction is treated as negligible, so the only horizontal forces acting are the arrows you draw.
On the already-moving crate, place two equal and opposite horizontal force arrows and adjust their lengths so they are exactly balanced (zero resultant).
Predict what the already-moving crate will do BEFORE releasing: will it stop, slow down, or keep moving at the same speed? State your reasoning.
Observe the crate: with balanced forces (zero resultant) it keeps gliding to the right at a steady speed rather than stopping.

Now make the RIGHTWARD arrow longer than the leftward one, so the resultant points right — the same direction the crate is already moving — and watch it accelerate; keep that arrow stretched and notice its SPEED keeps climbing for as long as the unbalanced force acts along the motion.
View an overlay showing a single resultant arrow that REPLACES the separate arrows (not drawn in addition to them).

Switch to the non-collinear mode: this clears the previous motion and sets the crate at rest. Place two arrows at an angle, join them head-to-tail to build the resultant geometrically, then watch the crate accelerate from rest along that resultant direction.
activities.title: Force-arrow playground: balanced forces that keep gliding

feedback: If you predicted 'lots of force, so it should move' or 'the stronger side's force is left over': equal and opposite pulls cancel to a zero resultant regardless of how hard each side pulls.
Skydiver at steady speed: weight down and air resistance up are equal, so the resultant is zero — yet she IS moving, at a constant speed. Zero resultant means no change, not stopped.
Braking car that is moving forwards: the resultant points backwards (opposite the forward motion) because the car is slowing down.
activities.intendedInsight: Large equal and opposite pulls still give a zero resultant; the size of the individual forces does not add up to a 'big leftover'. A zero resultant means no change in motion, so a steadily falling skydiver has a zero resultant yet is still moving, and a forwards-moving braking car has a backward resultant while still moving forwards.
learnerActions: Set up two students to pull a rope tied to a central marker; they will both pull hard and adjust until the marker holds still.
Before the pulling starts, predict: if both students pull hard and the marker is held still, what is the resultant on the marker? Does a big pull on each side mean a big resultant? Say WHY.
Observe that the marker can be held still even under large pulls, then explain in terms of the resultant why, while it stays still, the two pulls must be equal and opposite.
Discuss the skydiver case: during a steady (terminal-velocity) fall, state the resultant and whether she is moving.
Discuss a braking car that is still moving forwards: state which way the resultant points and why.
activities.title: Tug-of-war predict–observe–explain
